 4 Types of People Who Will Benefit Most From Social Security's 2027 COLA
 Paige Cerulli 2026년 11월 7일 토 오전 11:05 UTC 0 
The announcement of the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) means a boost in
Social Security senior benefits next year. Designed to help ensure benefits
retain their buying power and keep up with inflation, the COLA increases
benefits for nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries and about 7.3
million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI). However, certain
people stand to benefit more from the increased benefits than others.
Here's what you should know about how the COLA works, who may benefit from it
the most, and how it may affect your benefits.
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 How the COLA impacts benefits 
On October 14, the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced a 3.6% COLA
for 2027. The COLA is calculated using third-quarter Consumer Price Index for
Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) data. The COLA raises the
average retired-worker benefit from $2,095 in 2026 to about $2,170 in 2027.
Benefits don't increase by a uniform, flat rate. Instead, they increase by the
percentage determined by the COLA - in this case, 3.6%. Therefore, the size of a
beneficiary's benefit checks in 2026 directly affects the size of their increase
in 2027.
Certain groups of people may gain more than others from the COLA.

 High lifetime earners and those who delayed claiming benefits
Individuals whose benefit checks are larger should see a larger increase in
benefits from the COLA. For example, a $1,500 benefit should increase by about
$54 per month, but a $2,000 benefit should increase by about $72.
Social Security benefits are calculated based on an individual's earnings, and
the SSA uses up to 35 years of earnings, including the highest indexed earnings,
in that formula. High lifetime earners who receive larger benefit checks stand
to receive a larger benefits bump than lower-earning individuals who receive
smaller checks.
Similarly, individuals who delayed claiming benefits may see a bigger boost
because of their larger checks. Individuals who wait to claim Social Security
until after their full retirement age receive delayed retirement credits that
help their benefits grow. For each year they don't claim, their monthly benefit
increases by about 8%. Once individuals reach age 70, their benefits stop
growing. Delaying benefits for even a year or two may result in a larger check,
and those individuals then receive a bigger boost from the COLA.
 Beneficiaries not enrolled in Medicare
Medicare increases may quickly eat into any extra benefits that the COLA
provides. For example, the Medicare Part B premium is projected to increase by
$6.60 to $209.50 per month in 2027. Since Part B premiums are taken out of
Social Security checks, they may start to erode the benefits before recipients
see the money.

Other costs are increasing, too. Though the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid
Services (CMS) projects that average premiums for Medicare Advantage plans may
fall in 2027, an Investopedia analysis of CMS data found that premiums may rise
in 19 states.
Social Security recipients who have other forms of health insurance may avoid
these increases and keep more of their benefits.

 SSI recipients
SSI recipients benefit slightly more simply because of timing. Social Security
recipients should see the boost from the COLA beginning in January 2027, but SSI
recipients should receive that boost just a bit earlier, on December 31, 2026.
Some individuals who receive both Social Security and SSI may see both types of
benefits increased by the COLA.
 Survivors and spouses
Survivors and spouses also stand to receive more benefits because of the COLA.
The COLA applies to survivor and spousal benefits the same way it applies to
workers' Social Security benefits.
 The people who gain the least from the COLA
Just as several groups of people stand to benefit more from the COLA, others may
benefit less. Individuals whose Medicare Part B premium increases significantly
may see that premium consume a large share of their check. That effect may be
worsened for low-income individuals who already received smaller benefit checks
and who, in turn, received a smaller COLA increase.
Households with a rising income that crosses an Income-Related Monthly
Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) or benefit-taxation threshold may also see minimal
benefit from the COLA. For example, up to 85% of an individual's Social Security
income may be taxable. If that individual's income climbs, they may be required
to pay extra tax on their benefits, reducing the amount they gain from the COLA.
The IRMAA, a surcharge that may be added to Medicare Part B and Part D premiums,
may also impact higher-income Medicare recipients. If those recipients' income
crosses certain thresholds, they may have to pay the IRMAA surcharge, which may
eat into any COLA increase.

 Bottom line
Though the COLA increases benefits for all beneficiaries, the effect isn't
uniform, and some people may benefit more from the increase than others. To find
out how your benefits may be affected, you may log into your my Social Security
account beginning in late November to receive a COLA notice that includes your
2027 benefit amounts. If you haven't signed up for paperless notices in my
Social Security, you'll receive your COLA notice by mail in December.
Once you know your 2027 Social Security amounts, you may want to revisit your
budget and your retirement
plan to make any adjustments needed.
